A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching material relocated between sections and appendices.

before.justification: V1 Section 4 and Figure 1 report original simulations comparing Algorithms 1 and 3 with optimal steady-state control.

after.justification: V2 Appendix B reports original simulation trajectories and an additional model-count experiment, including policy regret averaged over 40 independent realizations.

M1.justification: The posterior-based model selection, certainty-equivalent control, added excitation, packing routine, and parametric algorithm remain unchanged. Normalization constants, Gaussian covariance, and rejection sampling clarify existing procedures; v1 already restricted parametric sampling to the specified parameter set.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate online control of a 20-state, five-input linear leaky-integrator system using finite candidate models and a 500-parameter model family. The revised chain configuration and candidate counts are settings changes within this retained task.

E2.justification: Algorithms 1 and 3 and the known-dynamics optimal steady-state policy remain the evaluated comparison methods. V2 separates their displays and varies Algorithm 1's candidate count without introducing another comparator. Newly cited methods are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: The reported simulator changes from four five-dimensional chains to five four-dimensional chains. The parametric experiment's excitation formula replaces ln(p) with p, and parameter error is displayed without v1's normalization. V2 also introduces policy-regret evaluation across four candidate counts. These are substantive reported setting and protocol revisions; the PDFs do not establish which changes reflect reruns versus corrections.

E4.justification: V2 Appendix B.3 and Figure 3 add a focused scalability analysis varying candidate count over 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000. It examines how model count affects regret and state transients; v1 contains no corresponding sensitivity study.

E5.justification: V1 gives no repeated-run count or averaging procedure for its illustrative trajectories. V2 newly reports 40 independent realizations per candidate count and averages policy regret in Figure 3a. It does not add confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The trajectory results are replaced: v1 reports roughly 10 steps to near-optimal behavior for Algorithm 1, whereas v2 reports about 20 in the text and 25 in Figure 1's caption; Algorithm 3 remains around 60. These concern revised settings, not a controlled performance change. V2 adds model-count-dependent regret and state trajectories and removes the input-norm results.

T1.justification: V2 revises the origin and smoothness assumptions, introduces offset constants into the regret and state-moment analysis, and reformulates the policy-continuity assumptions. New Propositions D.1 and F.2 supply sufficient-condition arguments for policy stability and nonlinear excitation. The linear excitation bound and the unnormalized-loss step-size restrictions are also revised.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same three model classes, headline regret scalings, finite-time identification and state-moment guarantees, separation principle, and practical motivation. Additional evidence and comparisons with optimistic methods do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: V2 explains the Bellman inequality through dissipativity and discusses why an optimal average-cost Bellman equation need not exist. It also clarifies the role of Q-function minimization in policy stability and develops the connection between excitation and controllability. The broader applicability limitations remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 supplies the stage-cost formula, explicit system matrices, parameter sampling intervals, controller equations, MATLAB dlqr usage, Gaussian covariance and rejection-sampling details. Appendix B also adds hardware specifications, approximate runtime, and computational costs. Much of this makes the existing implementation more reproducible rather than establishing a changed algorithm.

R1.justification: The introduction and Appendix A substantially expand positioning against optimism and Eluder-dimension approaches and against model-ensemble reinforcement learning. Added discussions include Croissant et al., Doya et al., Rajeswaran et al., and Modi et al., alongside tabular reinforcement learning and dissipativity literature. This exceeds a citation-style update.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: the numerical section becomes Appendix B with setup, assumption, complexity, and results discussions; Algorithm 3 moves forward and Algorithm 2 moves into the appendix. The main model-selection proof sketch becomes an appendix pointer, while assumption explanations and related-work passages are extensively revised.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout and rearranges algorithm boxes. V1's combined three-panel figure becomes two separate two-panel trajectory figures, with changed scales, legends, and captions and no input panel. V2 adds a further two-panel scalability figure.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's brief simulation description, v2 makes the empirical work substantially easier to reproduce through explicit system, cost, controller, and sampling details. Its repeated-run scalability experiment provides targeted evidence for the model-count claim, and the expanded assumption discussions improve assessability. These are clear gains, although Appendix B introduces an incorrect S2 label for Algorithm 3 and retains a five-step-lag description despite specifying four-state chains.
